title: Robert Carver Ran a Multi-Billion Dollar Systematic Portfolio for Man AHL. Now He Invests Solo.

meta.source: General Transcripts/Robert Carver Ran a Multi-Billion Dollar Systematic Portfolio for Man AHL. Now He Invests Solo..docx

speakers: Robert Carver (independent systematic futures trader, ex-Man AHL head of fixed income, author)
summary:
Odds on Open interview (July 2025) with Rob Carver on running billions at Man AHL and trading solo.
Approach: slow diversified systematic futures (trend, carry, skew, relative value) earning risk premia, not inefficiencies; skepticism, explicit rather than implicit fitting, realistic backtests, and metrics beyond Sharpe (LTCM lesson); slow strategies make alpha decay undetectable; collaborative research review at AHL vs pod incentives.

coverage.note: P&L abstraction and the $1bn week at AHL
experience with losses; AHL culture; systematic trading needs less market watching
quant skill sets by trading frequency; hiring path dependence
skepticism as key trait; Sharpe ratio and LTCM question
LTCM, Sharpe limits, peso problem, geometric return and bootstrapping
push fitting into explicit process; realistic backtests; alpha decay
decay of trend; Carver's trading rules list
career advice (excluded); risk premia not inefficiencies
rate of adding signals, strike rate, small-account innovation, crude portfolio construction; AHL idea flow
AHL collaborative research process and formal veto
pod shop vs Man AHL structure and incentives

completeness_estimate: 0.92 - first reader extracted nearly every method point (Sharpe/LTCM, explicit versus implicit fitting, alpha decay, full list of trading rules, research review) accurately; missed founder-culture, institutional-incentive, pod-versus-collaborative and Man-is-not-a-pod-shop points plus the money-secondary hiring view.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: if you did look at your P&L, then then definitely look at it in in percentages rather than in actual number terms
claims.claim: Abstract P&L into percentages and ideally avoid looking at P&L to avoid emotional reactions; Carver's fixed income pool lost about 10-11% in the worst week, equivalent to $1bn at fund level.

correction.issue: The $1bn is the whole-fund loss that a newly hired colleague remarked on; Carver's own fixed income pool lost about 10-11% in that week. The two figures are not equivalent.
correction.fix: In its worst week Carver's fixed income pool lost about 10-11% while the whole fund lost roughly $1bn (a newcomer from a discretionary fund was shocked); thinking in percentages and not looking at P&L makes such losses easier to handle.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: The first the first time you experience that kind of loss um is is going to be harder than the the the the second, third, fourth, 10th, 20th time you've experienced it.
claims.claim: Experience of past market events (2008, COVID, April 2025 tariffs) makes large losses easier to stomach and expect.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: if you're trading systematically, then um, there's less need to be constantly observing the markets.
claims.claim: Systematic trading allows a more abstract, objective view without constantly following news.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: the more high frequency you're trading the more I think you can treat the market as an abstract object
claims.claim: Required skills depend on trading frequency: high-frequency needs programmers and data analysts, low-frequency macro needs broader market and economic knowledge.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: there is a degree of path dependence in that you know people will look at firms that have done well and say well what kind of people do they hire
claims.claim: Beliefs about what background makes the best quants may reflect path dependence from successful firms' hiring rather than causal skill.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: has ultimately been because people have been overconfident and have have trusted in their back test too much or assumed that their data was clean when it wasn't
claims.claim: Skepticism is the key trait: almost every error comes from overconfidence in backtests, unclean data or forward bias in prices.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: even with that disastrous event that caused them to lose basically all their capital, um LTCM still had a sharp ratio of over three
claims.claim: LTCM still had a Sharpe ratio above 3 after its collapse, so Sharpe is not an ideal metric; there are no ideal performance metrics.

correction.issue: Carver states the LTCM Sharpe figure from memory and says he has not checked it, so the number is low-confidence rather than a fact.
correction.fix: From memory (unchecked), LTCM still had a Sharpe ratio above 3 even including its final collapse, which Carver uses to show that Sharpe is not an ideal metric and that no performance metric is ideal.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: it's not appropriate to use a SH ratio to to judge their efficacy
claims.claim: Sharpe assumes symmetric, normal returns; LTCM-type strategies (option selling, CDS premium: small gains, rare disasters) are negatively skewed and should not be judged by Sharpe.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: their data sets weren't didn't go back long enough to see the outliers that would have killed them
claims.claim: LTCM's failure was the peso problem: data too short to include outliers; any metric including outliers would have shown too much leverage.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: for people who can't use leverage and therefore sharp ratio is is sort of secondary to a measure like say geometric return
claims.claim: Sharpe is the go-to metric for leveraged futures traders, but for unleveraged investors geometric return is more appropriate; maximising Sharpe maximises geometric return only under normality and free leverage.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: I'll look at it you know using say a bootstrapping technique and I'll use the distribution of those geometric returns
claims.claim: Carver evaluates geometric return via bootstrap and considers a conservative percentile of the distribution rather than the median.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: what you actually want is a portfolio of these parameters
claims.claim: Explicit fitting done right weights parameter sets by statistical evidence (slightly more for the best) instead of choosing one best parameter, using rolling or expanding windows.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: swapping out one model and swapping in another model. But having done so importantly with full knowledge of the road's performance of those two models
claims.claim: Implicit fitting: choosing models or removing markets after seeing the backtest uses future performance knowledge, undoing robust explicit fitting.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: to try and basically push as much as possible into the explicit fitting
claims.claim: Put all model choices into one explicit procedure where weights shift only as evidence accrues, giving a realistic backtest and avoiding choosing a model with hindsight.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: if your past performance is unrealistically high, then both of those decisions will have been stupid ones
claims.claim: Unrealistic backtest performance leads to excessive leverage (LTCM) and trading too fast with high costs, so a realistic backtest matters even if the final model is the same.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: if I was trading you know high frequency data I would expect my alpha decay to be have a halflife of about a month and a half or two months maybe
claims.claim: High-frequency alpha decays with half-life of 1.5-2 months and is detectable statistically in real time, requiring constant replacement.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: that decay process potentially happening with halflife of one or two decades uh which means it's almost impossible to distinguish it from the kind of just general statistical noise
claims.claim: For slow systems alpha decay with a half-life of 1-2 decades cannot be distinguished from noise, so it is not worth monitoring; basic trend following has decayed gradually over 50-60 years.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: because their performance is not that high to begin with, it's actually impossible to tell statistically whether that's the case
claims.claim: Pure trend following may have stopped working for a decade, but low Sharpe makes this undetectable statistically.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: Um, so I'd be less exposed to a decay in the performance of pure trend anyway.
claims.claim: Diversifying across many trading rules beyond pure trend reduces exposure to trend decay; slow trading lets Carver ignore decay.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: That's basically um a the a trend on a trend.
claims.claim: Acceleration rule: trend on trend; positive acceleration if momentum is increasing or a fall decelerates.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: my trend signal on the whole asset class rather than just an individual market
claims.claim: Asset-class trend: apply a trend signal on the whole asset class (are equities overall bullish) and go long all its markets.
claims.direction: long entire asset class when bullish

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: sees where a price is within a range and if it's near the extreme of that range then it goes longer or shorter
claims.claim: Breakout rule: go long or short when price is near the extreme of its range.
claims.direction: long near highs, short near lows

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: looks at the slope of the uh futures curve um see whether it's in contango or backquidation
claims.claim: Carry rule: positions based on futures curve slope (contango versus backwardation).

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: average crossover. So that's momentum on the actual price itself.
claims.claim: Momentum rule: exponentially weighted moving average crossover on price.
claims.direction: long when fast EWMA above slow

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: let's say the S&P has outperformed the the footsy 100 for the last couple of years then I would go short the S&P and long the footsen
claims.claim: Very slow relative mean reversion: assets mean revert at long horizons, so short the recent multi-year outperformer vs the laggard.
claims.direction: short past winner, long past loser (relative)

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: I can't seem to get those strategies to work after trading costs
claims.claim: Short-horizon mean reversion exists but does not survive trading costs for Carver.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: perform a risk normalization on the price series. So that makes the price series itself more normally distributed and gives a cleaner signal
claims.claim: Normalised momentum applies momentum to a risk-normalised price series, giving more normal distribution and cleaner signal.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: if the carry is higher in one particular part of the equities space say I you know go long that and short things with lower carry
claims.claim: Relative carry: long higher-carry and short lower-carry markets within an asset class.
claims.direction: long high carry, short low carry within asset class

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: So I go long things that have gone up relative to other things.
claims.claim: Relative momentum within asset classes: long recent relative winners; the opposite of slow mean reversion but at faster frequency.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: then I would actually go long those assets um because generally speaking the market pays a risk premium for assets like that
claims.claim: Skew rule: go long assets with recent extreme sharp falls (negative skew), absolute and relative, because the market pays a risk premium for them.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: I believe that basically all the money I make is from you know what an economist will call risk premier.
claims.claim: Carver believes his systematic returns are risk premia, not market inefficiencies, since the methods are public and long-existing.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: I might add like one thing a year on average if that maybe less.
claims.claim: Because he trades slowly with slow decay, Carver adds about one new signal a year or less, with a strike rate of about 20% of ideas researched, and prefers failing to overfitting.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: I'm still able to trade over 200 futures markets with a very small account with a relatively small account size
claims.claim: The main system innovation of the last decade was handling a small account while trading over 200 futures markets, unrelated to finding an edge.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: the way I do my construction is actually quite crude because that works just as well as the more sophisticated techniques
claims.claim: Crude portfolio construction works as well as sophisticated optimisation techniques.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: any any research report that was written um anyone from the kind of quant team could go and look could go and read that
claims.claim: At AHL a shared research library avoided redoing earlier work and allowed building on it, with seminars including traders and middle office to catch practical flaws.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: the head of risk and the CIO had to kind of um they basically had the right of veto on these things
claims.claim: Formal proposals for new strategies needed review by head of risk and CIO with veto; this rigour was valuable though mistakes still happened.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: because of the pod structure, the compensation structure, you're going to take home a bigger percentage of your revenue
claims.claim: Pod shops pay a larger share of P&L to profitable teams and fire losers, attracting money-motivated people, while collaborative firms like Man AHL attract others.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: firms sort of have carry the DNA of their founders within them
claims.claim: A firm's research culture follows its founders: AHL was founded by three physicists and outsiders who took a scientific outside view of markets, whereas many US CTAs came from pit-trading lineage with a more visceral, intuitive market understanding; each approach has strengths and weaknesses.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: working in institution I had to justify my salary right so I had to generate new ideas even if arguably they weren't necessary
claims.claim: Institutional incentives push researchers to keep producing new signals even when the existing slow, high-alpha system does not need them, which raises complexity and overfitting risk; an independent slow trader has no such pressure.
claims.conditions: applies to low-frequency systems with slow decay

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: a kind of collaborative environment compared to say like a pod shop where people are very much in their own silos and they literally don't want to leak any information to the desk next to them
claims.claim: Pod shops run teams in information silos that compete and share nothing, while a collaborative quant firm shares research openly, which avoids duplicated work and lets ideas be checked by others.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: I'm not sure I'd put manh in the same bucket as to millennial. So you know they're not a pod shop.
claims.claim: Corrects the host's premise: Man Group is a public company owning several hedge funds, none of them pod shops, and AHL has only about 100-120 front-office staff, so the talent-and-capital consolidation argument about Citadel and Millennium does not apply directly to it.

claims.speaker: Robert Carver
claims.quote: I think the people you want working for you are those for whom money is a secondary consideration
claims.claim: Beyond a certain pay level extra money does not matter to most people, so the best quant hires are those motivated by culture and the work rather than money; the same applies to AI researchers offered nine-figure packages.
